claim: Escherichia coli single-stranded (ss)DNA binding (SSB) protein mediates genome maintenance processes by regulating access to ssDNA.
source: Escherichia coli single-stranded (ss)DNA binding (SSB) protein mediates genome maintenance processes by regulating access to ssDNA.
evidence: This is a statement from the abstract summarizing the general function of SSB protein.

claim: E. coli SSB is a homotetrameric protein that wraps ssDNA in multiple distinct binding modes.
source: This homotetrameric protein wraps ssDNA in multiple distinct binding modes that may be used selectively in different DNA processes, and whose detailed wrapping topologies remain speculative.
evidence: This statement is supported by references to prior ensemble studies and the structural characterization presented in the manuscript.

claim: The detailed wrapping topologies of SSB binding modes remain speculative.
source: This homotetrameric protein wraps ssDNA in multiple distinct binding modes that may be used selectively in different DNA processes, and whose detailed wrapping topologies remain speculative.
evidence: The authors explicitly state that the detailed wrapping topologies are not fully known prior to this study.

claim: Stretching a single ssDNA-SSB complex reveals discrete states that correlate with known binding modes.
source: Stretching a single ssDNA-SSB complex reveals discrete states that correlate with known binding modes, the likely ssDNA conformations and diffusion dynamics in each, and the kinetic pathways by which the protein wraps ssDNA and is dissociated.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data presented in Figures 2 and 3 showing discrete extension changes corresponding to different binding modes.

claim: The unwrapping energy costs increase the more ssDNA is unraveled from SSB.
source: The data allow us to construct an energy landscape for the ssDNA-SSB complex, revealing that unwrapping energy costs increase the more ssDNA is unraveled.
evidence: This is supported by the energy landscape analysis in Figure 6 showing unbalanced energy density.

claim: EcoSSB is an essential protein involved in most aspects of genome maintenance.
source: Escherichia coli single-stranded DNA binding protein (EcoSSB) is an essential protein involved in most aspects of genome maintenance (Meyer and Laine, 1990; Lohman and Ferrari, 1994; Shereda et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: EcoSSB binds with high affinity and little sequence specificity to single stranded DNA.
source: It binds with high affinity and little sequence specificity (Lohman and Overman, 1985; Lohman and Ferrari, 1994) to single stranded (ss)DNA intermediates formed during DNA replication, recombination, and repair, protecting them from both nucleolytic and chemical damage.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior biochemical studies.

claim: SSB protects ssDNA from both nucleolytic and chemical damage.
source: It binds with high affinity and little sequence specificity (Lohman and Overman, 1985; Lohman and Ferrari, 1994) to single stranded (ss)DNA intermediates formed during DNA replication, recombination, and repair, protecting them from both nucleolytic and chemical damage.
evidence: This is a known function of SSB supported by prior literature.

claim: SSB interacts directly with more than a dozen proteins involved in genome maintenance.
source: SSB also interacts directly with more than a dozen proteins involved in genome maintenance, regulating their access to ssDNA and bringing them to their sites of action (Shereda et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a review article.

claim: EcoSSB consists of four identical subunits of approximately 19 kDa each that form a functional tetramer.
source: It consists of four identical subunits (∼19 kDa each) that form a functional tetramer (Raghunathan et al., 1997, 2000) (Figure 1A) that is stable over a wide range of solution conditions and at sub-nanomolar protein concentrations (Lohman and Overman, 1985; Bujalowski and Lohman, 1991b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to structural studies and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The EcoSSB tetramer is stable over a wide range of solution conditions and at sub-nanomolar protein concentrations.
source: It consists of four identical subunits (∼19 kDa each) that form a functional tetramer (Raghunathan et al., 1997, 2000) (Figure 1A) that is stable over a wide range of solution conditions and at sub-nanomolar protein concentrations (Lohman and Overman, 1985; Bujalowski and Lohman, 1991b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior biochemical characterization studies.

claim: Each SSB monomer contains an oligonucleotide/oligosaccharide binding (OB) fold that contains the ssDNA binding site.
source: Each monomer contains an oligonucleotide/oligosaccharide binding (OB) fold that contains the ssDNA binding site (Raghunathan et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to the crystal structure study.

claim: EcoSSB tetramers bind and wrap ssDNA in a variety of binding modes that differ primarily in the number of OB folds that interact with the tetramer.
source: Thermodynamic studies have shown that EcoSSB tetramers bind and wrap ssDNA in a variety of binding modes that differ primarily in the number of OB folds that interact with the tetramer (Lohman and Ferrari, 1994).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior thermodynamic studies.

claim: Three different binding modes have been identified on poly(dT) at 25°C, termed (SSB)65, (SSB)56 and (SSB)35, which occlude 65, 56, and 35 nucleotides per tetramer, respectively.
source: Three different binding modes have been identified on poly(dT) at 25°C, termed (SSB)65, (SSB)56 and (SSB)35, which occlude 65, 56, and 35 nucleotides (nt) per tetramer, respectively, with a fourth mode observed at 37°C that occludes 40 nt (Bujalowski and Lohman, 1986).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior ensemble studies.

claim: A fourth SSB binding mode is observed at 37°C that occludes 40 nt.
source: Three different binding modes have been identified on poly(dT) at 25°C, termed (SSB)65, (SSB)56 and (SSB)35, which occlude 65, 56, and 35 nucleotides (nt) per tetramer, respectively, with a fourth mode observed at 37°C that occludes 40 nt (Bujalowski and Lohman, 1986).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior ensemble studies.

claim: SSB binding modes can reversibly interconvert, with transitions influenced primarily by salt concentration and type as well as protein binding density on the DNA.
source: These modes can reversibly interconvert, with the transitions influenced primarily by salt concentration and type as well as protein binding density on the DNA (Bujalowski and Lohman, 1986).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior ensemble studies.

claim: The (SSB)35 mode binds ssDNA with high cooperativity, forming protein clusters.
source: The (SSB)35 mode also binds ssDNA with high cooperativity, forming protein clusters (Sigal et al., 1972; Ruyechan and Wetmur, 1975; Lohman et al., 1986; Kozlov et al., 2015) that may be important during DNA replication (Lohman et al., 1988).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior studies.

claim: SSB protein clusters in the (SSB)35 mode may be important during DNA replication.
source: The (SSB)35 mode also binds ssDNA with high cooperativity, forming protein clusters (Sigal et al., 1972; Ruyechan and Wetmur, 1975; Lohman et al., 1986; Kozlov et al., 2015) that may be important during DNA replication (Lohman et al., 1988).
evidence: This is a speculative claim supported by a citation.

claim: SSB utilizes all of its binding modes during its different roles in genome maintenance.
source: It has been suggested that SSB utilizes all of these binding modes during its different roles in genome maintenance (Lohman et al., 1988) and that transitions between modes may control access of other proteins to the ssDNA (Wessel et al., 2013; Bhattacharyya et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Transitions between SSB binding modes may control access of other proteins to the ssDNA.
source: It has been suggested that SSB utilizes all of these binding modes during its different roles in genome maintenance (Lohman et al., 1988) and that transitions between modes may control access of other proteins to the ssDNA (Wessel et al., 2013; Bhattacharyya et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The crystal structure of SSB with bound ssDNA suggests a model for the (SSB)65 mode in which 65 nt of ssDNA wrap around an SSB tetramer in a topology resembling the seams on a baseball.
source: Crystallographic studies of a C-terminal truncation of the SSB tetramer (SSBc) with two molecules of (dC)35 bound suggest a model for the (SSB)65 mode in which 65 nt of ssDNA wrap around an SSB tetramer in a topology resembling the seams on a baseball (Raghunathan et al., 2000) (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to the crystal structure study and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: A model for the (SSB)35 mode has been proposed based on the crystal structure.
source: Based on this structure, a model for the (SSB)35 mode has also been proposed (Raghunathan et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to the crystal structure study.

claim: Less is known about the wrapping configurations of the (SSB)56 mode compared to other binding modes.
source: Less is known about the wrapping configurations of the other binding modes, especially the (SSB)56 mode that has only been detected on long poly(dT) ssDNA (Bujalowski and Lohman, 1986).
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field.

claim: The (SSB)56 mode has only been detected on long poly(dT) ssDNA.
source: Less is known about the wrapping configurations of the other binding modes, especially the (SSB)56 mode that has only been detected on long poly(dT) ssDNA (Bujalowski and Lohman, 1986).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior ensemble studies.

claim: Single-molecule FRET measurements characterized transitions between SSB binding modes.
source: Single-molecule FRET (smFRET) measurements characterized transitions between binding modes (Roy et al., 2007) and established that EcoSSB tetramers can diffuse along ssDNA (Roy et al., 2009) by a reptation mechanism (Zhou et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior single-molecule studies.

claim: EcoSSB tetramers can diffuse along ssDNA by a reptation mechanism.
source: Single-molecule FRET (smFRET) measurements characterized transitions between binding modes (Roy et al., 2007) and established that EcoSSB tetramers can diffuse along ssDNA (Roy et al., 2009) by a reptation mechanism (Zhou et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior single-molecule studies.

claim: Force gradually unravels ssDNA from EcoSSB.
source: Using a combination of optical traps and smFRET, Zhou et al. (2011) showed that force gradually unravels ssDNA from EcoSSB and proposed that the energy landscape for SSB-ssDNA interactions is smooth, with few barriers to unwrapping.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a prior study.

claim: The energy landscape for SSB-ssDNA interactions was previously proposed to be smooth, with few barriers to unwrapping.
source: Using a combination of optical traps and smFRET, Zhou et al. (2011) showed that force gradually unravels ssDNA from EcoSSB and proposed that the energy landscape for SSB-ssDNA interactions is smooth, with few barriers to unwrapping.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a prior study, which the current manuscript contradicts.

claim: The ssDNA exhibits discrete wrapping states consistent with the known (SSB)65, (SSB)56 and (SSB)35 binding modes when mechanical force is applied.
source: Applying mechanical force to destabilize the SSB-ssDNA complex and facilitate transitions between binding modes, we show that the ssDNA exhibits discrete wrapping states consistent with the known (SSB)65, (SSB)56 and (SSB)35 binding modes.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: The experimental results are compatible with putative models of the (SSB)35 structure.
source: Our results are compatible with putative models of the (SSB)35 structure (Raghunathan et al., 2000) and reveal a likely wrapping configuration for the (SSB)56 mode.
evidence: This claim is supported by the structural modeling analysis in Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: The study reveals a likely wrapping configuration for the (SSB)56 mode.
source: Our results are compatible with putative models of the (SSB)35 structure (Raghunathan et al., 2000) and reveal a likely wrapping configuration for the (SSB)56 mode.
evidence: This claim is supported by the structural modeling analysis in Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: SSB-(dT)70 complexes exhibit reversible force-induced transitions between modes without dissociation.
source: SSB-(dT)70 complexes exhibit reversible force-induced transitions between modes without dissociation and SSB can diffuse along ssDNA in the different binding modes, indicating a highly dynamic complex.
evidence: This claim is supported by the constant force experiments shown in Figure 2.

claim: SSB can diffuse along ssDNA in the different binding modes.
source: SSB-(dT)70 complexes exhibit reversible force-induced transitions between modes without dissociation and SSB can diffuse along ssDNA in the different binding modes, indicating a highly dynamic complex.
evidence: This claim is supported by the combined FRET and force measurements shown in Figure 4.

claim: The SSB-ssDNA complex is highly dynamic.
source: SSB-(dT)70 complexes exhibit reversible force-induced transitions between modes without dissociation and SSB can diffuse along ssDNA in the different binding modes, indicating a highly dynamic complex.
evidence: This is inferred from the observed transitions and diffusion behavior.

claim: The energy landscape for SSB-ssDNA interactions contains multiple barriers between discrete wrapping conformations.
source: In contrast to previous suggestions (Zhou et al., 2011), the landscape contains multiple barriers between discrete wrapping conformations, suggesting a distinct wrapping pathway for EcoSSB.
evidence: This claim is supported by the energy landscape analysis in Figure 6.

claim: The energy cost of unwrapping SSB increases as ssDNA is unraveled from its ends.
source: Moreover, the energy density is unbalanced, such that the energy cost of unwrapping increases as ssDNA is unraveled from its ends.
evidence: This claim is supported by the energy landscape analysis in Figure 6.

claim: The energy density of SSB-ssDNA wrapping is unbalanced.
source: Moreover, the energy density is unbalanced, such that the energy cost of unwrapping increases as ssDNA is unraveled from its ends.
evidence: This claim is supported by the energy landscape analysis in Figure 6.

claim: The DNA construct used consists of a 70-nt poly(dT) ssDNA segment flanked by two long double-stranded DNA handles.
source: As shown in Figure 1B, two trapped functionalized micron-sized beads were tethered together by a DNA construct consisting of a 70-nt poly(dT) ssDNA segment flanked by two long double-stranded DNA (dsDNA) 'handles' ('Materials and methods').
evidence: This is a description of the experimental construct shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The length of the ssDNA was chosen to accommodate one SSB tetramer in its (SSB)65 binding mode.
source: The length of the ssDNA was chosen to accommodate one SSB tetramer in its (SSB)65 binding mode.
evidence: This is an explicit statement about the experimental design.

claim: Experiments were performed under salt conditions and protein concentrations known to favor the (SSB)65 mode in the absence of mechanical tension.
source: We also worked under salt conditions and protein concentrations known to favor the (SSB)65 mode in the absence of mechanical tension (Bujalowski and Lohman, 1986; Roy et al., 2007) ('Materials and methods').
evidence: This is an explicit statement about the experimental conditions, supported by citations.

claim: Force-extension curves of the DNA construct in the absence of protein were in excellent agreement with theoretical models of DNA elasticity.
source: Force-extension curves (FECs) of this construct in the absence of protein (Figure 1—figure supplement 1, green) were in excellent agreement with theoretical models of DNA elasticity ('Materials and methods'; Figure 1—figure supplement 1, black dashed line).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Upon stretching to a force >20 pN and relaxing the molecule, the FECs matched those in the absence of protein, indicating that the SSB had dissociated during the stretching process.
source: Upon stretching to a force >20 pN and relaxing the molecule, the FECs (Figure 1, red) matched those in the absence of protein (Figure 1—figure supplement 1, green), indicating that the SSB had dissociated during the stretching process.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 1.

claim: A single SSB was loaded onto the DNA and dissociated at high force, as confirmed by simultaneous fluorescence detection of dye labeled protein.
source: We confirmed that a single SSB was loaded onto the DNA and dissociated at high force through simultaneous fluorescence detection of dye labeled protein.
evidence: This claim is supported by the combined fluorescence and force measurements shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: The average dissociation force of SSB from ssDNA was 10.3 ± 0.9 pN.
source: The average dissociation force was 10.3 ± 0.9 pN, consistent with previous reports (Zhou et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a direct measurement from the experiments, supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The SSB-ssDNA wrapping free energy is 22 ± 2 kBT.
source: Integrating the area between protein-bound and bare FECs to the force at which the complex spends half its time bound and half unbound yielded a value for the SSB-ssDNA wrapping free energy of 22 ± 2 kBT ('Materials and methods') similar to a previously reported value (Zhou et al., 2011).
evidence: This is calculated from the experimental data and consistent with prior measurements.

claim: At tensions <1 pN, the data is consistent with 65 nt being wrapped around SSB.
source: The agreement between model and data at tensions <1 pN is consistent with 65 nt being wrapped around SSB at low forces.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of data to the model in Figure 1E.

claim: Beyond 1 pN force, the SSB wraps <65 nt of ssDNA.
source: Beyond this force, however, Δx is consistently below the prediction, indicating that the SSB wraps <65 nt of ssDNA, in agreement with earlier measurements (Zhou et al., 2011).
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of data to the model in Figure 1E and supported by citation.

claim: At low tensions (<3 pN), individual SSBs bind and compact ssDNA in a single step.
source: At low tensions (<3 pN), we observed that individual SSBs bind and compact ssDNA in a single step (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the constant force experiments shown in Figure 2B.

claim: SSBs remained bound to the ssDNA indefinitely at tensions below 3 pN.
source: SSBs remained bound to the ssDNA indefinitely at these tensions.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the constant force experiments.

claim: At higher tensions (3–8 pN), multiple steps upon SSB binding were observed, with dynamic transitions among 2 to 3 distinct states.
source: In contrast, at higher tensions, (3–8 pN), we observed multiple steps upon SSB binding, with dynamic transitions among 2 to 3 distinct states (Figure 2B, dashed lines) depending on tension, but no dissociation of SSB.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the constant force experiments shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Dynamic changes in extension at 3-8 pN represent wrapping and unwrapping transitions between intermediate conformations of a single ssDNA-SSB complex.
source: We interpret these dynamic changes in extension as wrapping and unwrapping transitions between intermediate conformations of a single ssDNA-SSB complex.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the observed dynamics, supported by fluorescence measurements.

claim: A single SSB tetramer was responsible for the observed wrapping-unwrapping dynamics, as corroborated by measurements of fluorescently labeled SSB.
source: We corroborated this interpretation with measurements of fluorescently labeled SSBf. Figure 2—figure supplement 1 shows that a single SSB tetramer was responsible for the observed wrapping-unwrapping dynamics.
evidence: This is supported by the combined fluorescence and force measurements shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Near the dissociation force (9–10 pN), multiple instances of one-step wrapping followed by complete release of ssDNA were observed.
source: Near the dissociation force (9–10 pN), we observed multiple instances of one-step wrapping followed by complete release of ssDNA.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the constant force experiments.

claim: At forces of 9-10 pN, SSB is unable to bind the DNA tether stably, and the observed transitions correspond to protein binding and dissociation.
source: At these forces, SSB is unable to bind the DNA tether stably, and the observed transitions correspond to protein binding and dissociation.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the observed dynamics at high forces, confirmed by fluorescence measurements.

claim: The amount of ssDNA wrapped by SSB decreases as tension increases.
source: Similarly to the force-ramp results, Δx decreases as tension increases, indicating that the amount of ssDNA wrapped by SSB decreases.
evidence: This is inferred from the extension change distributions shown in Figure 2C.

claim: SSB spends different amounts of time in particular wrapping states depending on tension.
source: The areas under the peaks in the distributions indicate that SSB spends different amounts of time in these particular states.
evidence: This is inferred from the extension change distributions shown in Figure 2C.

claim: As tension is increased, the SSB-ssDNA complex shifts to states with smaller extension changes, corresponding to lower extents of ssDNA wrapping.
source: As tension is increased, the SSB-ssDNA complex shifts to states with smaller Δx, corresponding to lower extents of ssDNA wrapping.
evidence: This is inferred from the extension change distributions shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The intermediate DNA wrapping states correspond to the different SSB binding modes observed on poly(dT) in ensemble measurements.
source: We considered the possibility that these intermediate DNA wrapping states correspond to the different SSB binding modes observed on poly(dT) in ensemble measurements (Bujalowski and Lohman, 1986).
evidence: This is a hypothesis tested by the structural modeling analysis in Figure 3.

claim: Data points in the extension change measurements are clustered into 4 groups corresponding to SSB wrapping approximately 65, 56, 35, and 17 nt.
source: Data points are clustered into 4 groups corresponding to those states (purple, blue, green, and red circles).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3A where data points are grouped based on the modeling analysis.

claim: The (SSB)56 mode has ssDNA bound to all four subunits, but with the 3′ terminal ssDNA end unraveled to the nearest hotspot.
source: They also suggest that the (SSB)56 mode has ssDNA bound to all four subunits, but with the 3′ terminal ssDNA end unraveled to the nearest hotspot (Figure 3C; schematic, and Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a structural model proposed based on the experimental data and modeling analysis.

claim: All 4 monomers of an SSB tetramer interact with ssDNA upon binding a molecule of (dT)56.
source: This model is consistent with studies (Bujalowski and Lohman, 1989a, 1989b) suggesting that all 4 monomers of an SSB tetramer interact with ssDNA upon binding a molecule of (dT)56.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior biochemical studies.

claim: At forces in the range of 5–8 pN, between 1 to 3 separate states wrapping 30–40 nt are observed.
source: At forces in the range of 5–8 pN, we observe between 1 to 3 separate states wrapping 30–40 nt.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the constant force experiments.

claim: At least two conformations wrapping approximately 35 nt are consistent with the observed extension changes.
source: We believe at least two conformations wrapping ∼35 nt are consistent with the observed extension changes, one of which is nearly identical to the proposed (SSB)35 structure (Raghunathan et al., 2000) (Figure 3C schematic, and Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is inferred from the modeling analysis shown in Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: An alternate '(SSB)35b' mode that occludes 35 nt but is structurally distinct from (SSB)35 has been suggested to exist.
source: Interestingly, prior studies (Roy et al., 2007) have suggested the existence of an alternate '(SSB)35b' mode that occludes 35 nt but is structurally distinct from (SSB)35, consistent with our observations.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a prior study.

claim: At tensions >8 pN, a stable intermediate reflecting approximately 17 nt of bound ssDNA was observed.
source: At tensions >8 pN, we also observed a stable intermediate reflecting ∼17 nt of bound ssDNA (Bujalowski and Lohman, 1989a, 1989b, 1991b).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the constant force experiments, supported by citations.

claim: A multitude of wrapping conformations around two monomers is consistent with the data for the approximately 17 nt intermediate.
source: Here, a multitude of wrapping conformations around two monomers is consistent with the data (Figure 3C schematic, and Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is inferred from the modeling analysis shown in Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Fluorescence quenching studies suggest that (dT)16 would bind to one monomer of SSB.
source: Although fluorescence quenching studies (Bujalowski and Lohman, 1991a) suggest that (dT)16 would bind to one monomer of SSB, partial interactions with two monomers in our structural model may sum to those of a monomer.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a prior study.

claim: Near dissociation, wrapping geometries could be more heterogeneous.
source: It is possible that near dissociation, wrapping geometries could be more heterogeneous.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the observations.

claim: EcoSSB can bind to ssDNA as short as (dT)8.
source: Prior studies have shown that EcoSSB can bind to ssDNA as short as (dT)8 (Krauss et al., 1981).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a prior study.

claim: Long-lived intermediates wrapping less than approximately 17 nt before SSB dissociation were not observed.
source: However, we do not observe long-lived intermediates wrapping less than ∼17 nt before SSB dissociation.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experiments.

claim: Almost every transition (98%) occurs between adjacent wrapping states.
source: Analyzing the transitions between wrapping intermediates (Figure 2B) reveals that almost every transition (N = 373 out of 380 total, 98%) occurs between adjacent wrapping states, that is, between (SSB)56 and (SSB)35, but never directly between (SSB)56 and (SSB)17.
evidence: This is a quantitative analysis of the transition data from Figure 2B.

claim: The observations suggest a single, linear kinetic pathway for wrapping and unwrapping.
source: This suggests a single, linear kinetic pathway for wrapping (Figure 3—figure supplement 2, right to left) and unwrapping (left to right).
evidence: This is inferred from the analysis of transition pathways.

claim: The proposed wrapping/unwrapping pathway is corroborated by measurements of E. coli SSB in competition with RecA for ssDNA.
source: This proposed pathway is corroborated by measurements of E. coli SSB in competition with RecA for ssDNA.
evidence: This is supported by the RecA competition experiments shown in Figure 5.

claim: In the absence of SSB, RecA extends the DNA construct by approximately 10 nm as it fills the ssDNA.
source: In the absence of SSB, RecA extends the construct by ∼10 nm as it fills the ssDNA (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), consistent with previous reports that ssDNA-RecA filaments are 50% longer than dsDNA (Hegner et al., 1999; Galletto et al., 2006) ('Materials and methods').
evidence: This is a direct observation from the RecA experiments, supported by citations.

claim: ssDNA-RecA filaments are 50% longer than dsDNA.
source: In the absence of SSB, RecA extends the construct by ∼10 nm as it fills the ssDNA (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), consistent with previous reports that ssDNA-RecA filaments are 50% longer than dsDNA (Hegner et al., 1999; Galletto et al., 2006) ('Materials and methods').
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: When RecA is added to ssDNA wrapped by a single SSB, RecA takes longer to polymerize but eventually removes the SSB in a stepwise fashion.
source: When RecA is added to ssDNA wrapped by a single SSB, RecA takes longer to polymerize but eventually removes the SSB in a stepwise fashion (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the RecA competition experiments shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The SSB is unraveled by RecA in discrete steps, corresponding to the pathway (SSB)35 → (SSB)17 → unbound.
source: Analyzing the measured extension changes from many measurements (Figure 5D; 'Materials and methods') reveals that the SSB is unraveled in discrete steps, corresponding to the same pathway of intermediates, (SSB)35 → (SSB)17 → unbound, as proposed above (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is inferred from the analysis of the RecA competition data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The free energy of wrapping into the (SSB)65 mode is 21 ± 1 kBT.
source: Our analysis (Figure 6) shows that the free energy of wrapping into the (SSB)65 mode is 21 ± 1 kBT, in excellent agreement with the area between protein-bound and bare FECs (22 ± 2 kBT; Figure 1D).
evidence: This is calculated from the energy landscape analysis shown in Figure 6.

claim: 73% of the wrapping energy is concentrated in the first 35 nt wrapped.
source: Interestingly, this wrapping free energy is not distributed evenly among the 65 nt. Instead, we find that 73% of the energy is concentrated in the first 35 nt wrapped (energy density = 0.44 ± 0.02 kBT/nt).
evidence: This is calculated from the energy landscape analysis shown in Figure 6.

claim: The energy density for the first 35 nt wrapped is 0.44 ± 0.02 kBT/nt.
source: Instead, we find that 73% of the energy is concentrated in the first 35 nt wrapped (energy density = 0.44 ± 0.02 kBT/nt).
evidence: This is calculated from the energy landscape analysis.

claim: The (SSB)65 and (SSB)56 states are separated by only approximately 0.7 kBT.
source: In contrast, the (SSB)65 and (SSB)56 states are separated by only ∼0.7 kBT (energy density ∼0.07 kBT/nt).
evidence: This is calculated from the energy landscape analysis shown in Figure 6.

claim: The energy density between (SSB)65 and (SSB)56 states is approximately 0.07 kBT/nt.
source: In contrast, the (SSB)65 and (SSB)56 states are separated by only ∼0.7 kBT (energy density ∼0.07 kBT/nt).
evidence: This is calculated from the energy landscape analysis.

claim: The last approximately 10 nt wrapped are more susceptible to unraveling and might be more accessible to other proteins competing for ssDNA.
source: This finding suggests that the last ∼10 nt wrapped are more susceptible to unraveling and thus might be more accessible to other proteins competing for ssDNA.
evidence: This is inferred from the unbalanced energy density profile.

claim: The unbalanced energy density profile may provide a mechanism by which SSB is displaced by the recombinase RecA.
source: This unbalanced energy density profile may provide a mechanism by which SSB is displaced by the recombinase RecA, which requires a foothold of 6–17 nt to polymerize into filaments (Joo et al., 2006; Bell et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the energy landscape analysis and supported by citations.

claim: RecA requires a foothold of 6–17 nt to polymerize into filaments.
source: This unbalanced energy density profile may provide a mechanism by which SSB is displaced by the recombinase RecA, which requires a foothold of 6–17 nt to polymerize into filaments (Joo et al., 2006; Bell et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: RecA filaments form only once the SSB transitions to the (SSB)35 mode, granting access to >14 nt of ssDNA.
source: We note that in the RecA/SSB competition experiment (Figure 5), we observe RecA filaments forming only once the SSB transitions to the (SSB)35 mode, granting access to >14 nt of ssDNA.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the RecA competition experiments shown in Figure 5.

claim: SSB can diffuse on ssDNA while in different wrapping modes.
source: Our measurements that SSB can diffuse on ssDNA while in different wrapping modes provide insights into how SSBs could be redistributed along ssDNA by other proteins seeking access to ssDNA.
evidence: This is supported by the combined FRET and force measurements shown in Figure 4.

claim: SSB-ssDNA rearrangements without unwrapping or rewrapping point to a sliding mechanism of diffusion in which ssDNA reptates along the protein.
source: The observation of SSB-ssDNA rearrangements without unwrapping or rewrapping (Figure 4) points to a sliding mechanism of diffusion in which ssDNA reptates along the protein, consistent with prior models (Zhou et al., 2011).
evidence: This is inferred from the FRET data shown in Figure 4 and supported by citation.

claim: RecA polymerization likely slides the SSB to one ssDNA-dsDNA junction prior to unravelling it.
source: In Figure 5, we believe RecA polymerization likely slides the SSB to one ssDNA-dsDNA junction prior to unravelling it (Roy et al., 2009; Bell et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the RecA competition data and supported by citations.

claim: Diffusion may be faster in the (SSB)35 mode than in the (SSB)56 mode.
source: Interestingly, the data in Figure 4 suggest that diffusion may be faster in the (SSB)35 mode.
evidence: This is inferred from the FRET transition rates shown in Figure 4.

claim: The transition rates between FRET states are approximately 1.8× larger in the (SSB)35 mode than in the (SSB)56 mode.
source: The transition rates between FRET states are ∼1.8× larger in the (SSB)35 mode than in the (SSB)56 mode.
evidence: This is calculated from the FRET data shown in Figure 4.

claim: A smaller site size leads to faster diffusion.
source: The observation that a smaller site size leads to faster diffusion is consistent with reports that human RPA, which covers 30 nt, has a larger diffusion coefficient than EcoSSB in its (SSB)65 mode (Nguyen et al., 2014).
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison to prior studies, supported by citation.

claim: Human RPA, which covers 30 nt, has a larger diffusion coefficient than EcoSSB in its (SSB)65 mode.
source: The observation that a smaller site size leads to faster diffusion is consistent with reports that human RPA, which covers 30 nt, has a larger diffusion coefficient than EcoSSB in its (SSB)65 mode (Nguyen et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a prior study.

claim: Different wrapping modes may be used selectively in different DNA metabolic processes.
source: Previous work has proposed that different wrapping modes may be used selectively in different DNA metabolic processes (e.g., replication vs recombination) (Sancar et al., 1981; Lohman et al., 1988).
evidence: This is a hypothesis from prior work, supported by citations.

claim: How and which SSB modes are used for particular processes remains unclear.
source: How and which of these modes are used for particular processes remains unclear, as experimental proof of this proposition has proven difficult to obtain in vitro.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field.

claim: The control of SSB wrapping mode by applied force may be a useful experimental tool to test the hypothesis that different modes are used for different processes.
source: We anticipate that the control of SSB wrapping mode by applied force may be a useful experimental tool to test this hypothesis.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about future applications of the technique.

claim: The diffusion constant for SSB in the (SSB)35 mode is approximately 27 nt²/s.
source: We reasoned that the lifetimes of the high FRET states in these traces correspond approximately to the time the protein takes to diffuse by one Förster radius from the ss-dsDNA junction, and estimated a diffusion constant D ≈ 27 nt2/s for the (SSB)35 mode and 15 nt2/s for the (SSB)56 mode.
evidence: This is estimated from the FRET lifetime data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The diffusion constant for SSB in the (SSB)56 mode is approximately 15 nt²/s.
source: We reasoned that the lifetimes of the high FRET states in these traces correspond approximately to the time the protein takes to diffuse by one Förster radius from the ss-dsDNA junction, and estimated a diffusion constant D ≈ 27 nt2/s for the (SSB)35 mode and 15 nt2/s for the (SSB)56 mode.
evidence: This is estimated from the FRET lifetime data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The estimated diffusion constants are consistent with prior reports when accounting for temperature and the expected reduction in D due to the 5 pN tension.
source: This range of values is consistent with prior reports (Roy et al., 2009) when accounting for temperature (∼23°C in our measurements) and the expected reduction in D due to the 5 pN tension (Roy et al., 2009; Zhou et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a comparison to prior measurements, supported by citations.

claim: No examples of transitions from state i → iii → ii (wrapping one end of DNA and releasing the other) were observed, providing no support for a 'rolling' mechanism of diffusion.
source: We observed no examples (0 of N = 82) of transitions from state i → iii → ii—wrapping one end of DNA and releasing the other—providing no support for a 'rolling' mechanism of diffusion (Romer et al., 1984) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative analysis of the FRET transition data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Mutation of Trp-54 to Ser disrupts interactions with ssDNA and favors wrapping in the (SSB)35 mode.
source: Mutation of Trp-54 to Ser was previously shown to disrupt interactions with ssDNA and favor wrapping in the (SSB)35 mode (Ferrari et al., 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a prior study.

claim: The number of nucleotides wrapped by the Trp-54 to Ser SSB mutant was lower than that of the wild type SSB, with Nw = 35 nt being the most probable wrapping conformation over the range of tensions assayed.
source: We similarly found that the number of nucleotides wrapped by this mutant was lower than that of the wild type SSB, with Nw = 35 nt being the most probable wrapping conformation over the range of tensions assayed (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the mutant SSB experiments shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: Trp-40, Trp-54, Trp-88 and Phe-60 play important roles in maintaining protein-DNA stability.
source: Trp-40, Trp-54, Trp-88 and Phe-60 have been shown to play important roles in maintaining protein-DNA stability (Casas-Finet et al., 1987; Khamis et al., 1987; Ferrari et al., 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior biochemical studies.

claim: Crystal structure analysis implicates Trp-54 and Arg-56 as important in creating pockets of positive electrostatic potential on the SSB surface for ssDNA to bind.
source: Crystal structure analysis also implicates Trp-54 and Arg-56 as important in creating pockets of positive electrostatic potential on the SSB surface for ssDNA to bind (Raghunathan et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to the crystal structure study.

claim: All-atom molecular dynamics simulations of SSB in solution with free oligonucleotides showed that DNA interacts most strongly to regions on each monomer near residues 54–56.
source: Lastly, a DNA density map generated by all-atom molecular dynamics (MDs) simulations of SSB (Maffeo, 2015) in solution with free oligonucleotides showed that DNA interacts most strongly to regions on each monomer near residues 54–56 (Trp-88 and Phe-60 are also located near this region) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1 right schematic, residues highlighted in green; 'Materials and methods').
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to MD simulations.

claim: The Trp-54/His-55/Arg-56 cluster was identified as a 'hotspot', residues on each SSB monomer that may serve as anchor points along the DNA wrapping path on the SSB.
source: Based on these results, we identified the Trp-54/His-55/Arg-56 cluster as a 'hotspot', residues on each SSB monomer that may serve as anchor points along the DNA wrapping path on the SSB.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on structural and MD simulation data.
